For the Father loves the Son, and embraces him with a singular love, the highest the equal, the eternal the coeternal, the one the only one. But he himself is bound to the Father by an affection no less: for love of whom he even dies, himself bearing witness when he says: 'That all may know that I love the Father, arise, let us go' (John 14:31); no doubt to the passion. That mutual knowledge, then, of the one who begets and of the one begotten, and their love likewise, what is it but a most sweet kiss, yet a most secret one?
8.2: For my part I judge that not even the angelic creature itself is admitted to so great and so holy a secret of the divine love. For, Paul being of this same mind, that peace surpasses every sense, even the angelic (Phil. 4:7). Whence she too, although presuming much, does not yet dare to say, 'Let him kiss me with his mouth,' reserving that, of course, to the Father alone: but asking something less: 'Let him kiss me,' she says, 'with the kiss of his mouth.' See the new bride receiving a new kiss, yet not from the mouth, but from the kiss of the mouth. 'He breathed on them,' it says — on the apostles, no doubt, that is, on the primitive Church — Jesus, and said: 'Receive the Holy Spirit' (John 20:22). It was surely a kiss. What? that bodily breath? No, but the invisible Spirit: who was given in that breath of the Lord for this reason, that by this it might be understood that he proceeds from him equally as from the Father, as truly the kiss, which is common to the one kissing and the one kissed. And so it suffices the bride if she is kissed by the kiss of the bridegroom, even if she is not kissed by the mouth. Nor does she think it a small or cheap thing to be kissed by the kiss: which is nothing other than to be filled with the Holy Spirit. For if the Father is rightly taken as the one kissing, and the Son as the one kissed, it will not be beside the point for the kiss to be understood as the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as he is the imperturbable peace of the Father and the Son, their firm bond, their undivided love, their indivisible unity.
8.3: It is of him, then, that the bride dares to speak, and it is he whom she confidently asks to be poured into her under the name of a kiss. For she holds something from which an occasion of presuming is not lacking. For when the Son says, 'No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son,' he added, 'or he to whom the Son shall have willed to reveal him.' But the bride does not distrust that he wills it for her, if he wills it for anyone. She asks boldly, therefore, that the kiss be given her, that is, that Spirit in whom both the Son is revealed to her and the Father. For the one without the other is by no means made known. Whence is that word: 'He who sees me sees my Father also' (John 14:9); and that of John, 'Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either.' 'But he who confesses the Son has the Father also' (1 John 2:23). From which it is clearly established that neither is the Father acknowledged without the Son, nor the Son without the Father. Rightly, then, does he place the height of blessedness not in the knowledge of one only, but of both, who says: 'This is eternal life, that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent' (John 17:3). And finally those who follow the Lamb are related to have his name, and the name of his Father, written on their foreheads (Rev. 14:1): which is to glory in the knowledge of both.
8.4: But someone says: 'Is the knowledge of the Holy Spirit, then, not necessary either, since, when he said that to know both the Father and the Son is eternal life, he was silent about the Holy Spirit?' It is, certainly: but where the Father and the Son are perfectly known, how is the goodness of both, which is the Holy Spirit, unknown? For neither does one man become fully known to another, so long as it lies hidden whether he is of a good or of an evil will. Although even when it was said, 'This is eternal life, that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent,' surely if that sending shows the good pleasure both of the Father kindly sending and of the Son willingly obeying, the Holy Spirit has not been altogether passed over in silence, where mention has been made of so great a grace of both. For the love and kindness of both is the Holy Spirit.
8.5: The bride asks, then, that the grace of this threefold knowledge be poured into her, as much indeed as can be received in mortal flesh, when she asks for the kiss. But she asks it of the Son, because it belongs to the Son to reveal to whom he has willed. The Son, therefore, reveals himself to whom he wills, and he reveals the Father also. But he reveals, without doubt, by the kiss, that is, by the Holy Spirit, the Apostle bearing witness, who says: 'But to us God has revealed them through his Spirit' (1 Cor. 2:10). But in giving the Spirit through whom he reveals, he reveals the Spirit himself as well; in giving he reveals, and in revealing he gives. Further, the revelation which comes about through the Holy Spirit not only enlightens unto knowledge, but also kindles unto love, Paul saying: 'The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us' (Rom. 5:5). And for this reason, perhaps, concerning those who, knowing God, did not glorify him as God, it is not read that they knew by the Holy Spirit revealing, because, although they knew, they did not love. For so you have it: 'For God revealed it to them.' Nor is it added, 'Through his Spirit,' lest impious minds should usurp for themselves the bride's kiss, which, content with that which puffs up, did not know that which builds up (1 Cor. 8:1). Let the Apostle himself, finally, say through what they knew. 'Through the things that have been made,' he says, 'they perceived them, being understood.' Whence it is also clear that they did not know perfectly him whom they did not love at all. For if they had known him fully, they would not have been ignorant of the goodness by which, for their redemption, he willed to be born and to die in the flesh. Hear, finally, what was revealed to them about God: 'His everlasting power,' he says, 'and divinity' (Rom. 1:19-21). You see that what belongs to loftiness, what belongs to majesty, they searched out in a presumption of spirit, not of God but of their own; but that he is meek and humble of heart, they did not understand. Nor is it wonderful, for their head Behemoth also [sees] nothing humble; but, as it is read of him, he sees everything that is high (Job 41:25). David, on the contrary, did not walk in great things, nor in wonders above himself (Ps. 131:1), lest the searcher of majesty be overwhelmed by glory (Prov. 25:27).
8.6: You also, that you may set your foot cautiously in hidden meanings, remember always what the Wise Man warns: 'Things higher than yourself,' he says, 'do not seek, and things stronger than yourself do not search into' (Sir. 3:22). Walk in the spirit in those things, and not in your own sense. The teaching of the Spirit does not sharpen curiosity, but kindles charity. Rightly, then, does the bride, seeking him whom her soul loves, not trust herself to the senses of her own flesh, nor rest in the empty reasonings of human curiosity; but she asks for a kiss, that is, she calls upon the Holy Spirit, through whom she may receive at once both a taste of knowledge and the seasoning of grace. And well is the knowledge which is given in a kiss received with love, because a kiss is a sign of love. Knowledge, therefore, which puffs up, since it is without charity, does not proceed from the kiss. But neither let those who have a zeal for God, and not according to knowledge, claim that for themselves in any way. For the grace of the kiss brings both gifts at once, both the light of knowledge and the fatness of devotion. For he is the Spirit of wisdom and of understanding, who, like a bee carrying wax and honey, has altogether both that with which to kindle the lamp of knowledge and that with which to pour in the savor of grace. Let neither, then, think that he has received the kiss, whether he who understands the truth and does not love it, or he who loves and does not understand. In this kiss, certainly, error has no place, nor lukewarmness. Wherefore, for the receiving of the twofold grace of the most holy kiss, let her who is the bride prepare over against it her two lips, the reason of understanding and the will of wisdom, so that, glorying in a full kiss, she may deserve to hear: 'Grace has been poured out upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever' (Ps. 45:2). And so the Father, kissing the Son, most fully pours out to him the secrets of his divinity, and breathes the sweetness of love, Scripture signifying this when it says: 'Day unto day pours out the word' (Ps. 19:2). To that embrace, certainly, eternal and singularly blessed, it is granted to no creature at all, as has already been said, to be present, the Spirit of both alone being witness and conscious of the mutual knowledge and love. For who has known the mind of the Lord? or who has been his counselor? (Rom. 11:34.)
8.7: But someone may perhaps say to me: 'From where, then, has it become known to you, which you confess has been entrusted to no creature?' Surely, 'The Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself has declared it' (John 1:18), I would say, not to me, wretched and unworthy, but plainly to John the friend of the bridegroom, whose words these are; and not to him alone, but also to John the evangelist, the disciple, certainly, whom Jesus loved. For his soul also was pleasing to God, worthy indeed of the name and the dowry of a bride, worthy of the bridegroom's embraces, worthy finally to recline upon the breast of the Lord. John drew from the bosom of the Only-begotten what that one had drawn from the Father. Nor he alone, however, but all those also to whom the angel of great counsel was saying the same thing: 'I have called you friends, because all things whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you' (John 15:15). Paul also drew it, whose gospel is not from man, nor did he receive it through man, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ (Gal. 1:11, 12). Surely all these can say, as happily as truly: 'The Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself has declared it to us.' And that declaring, what was it to them but a kiss? But a kiss from the kiss, and not from the mouth. Hear, indeed, the kiss from the mouth. 'I and the Father are one'; and again: 'I am in the Father, and the Father is in me' (John 10:30, 38). It is a kiss taken mouth to mouth; but no one draws near. A kiss, plainly, of love and of peace; but that love is above all knowledge, and that peace surpasses all sense. Nevertheless, what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man, God revealed to Paul through his Spirit, that is, through the kiss of his mouth. The Son, therefore, being in the Father, and the Father in the Son, is the kiss from the mouth. But that which is read: 'For we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know the things that have been given us by God' (1 Cor. 2:12), is surely the kiss from the kiss.
8.8: And that we may distinguish the one from the other more openly: he who receives the fullness takes the kiss from the mouth; but he who receives of the fullness receives the kiss from the kiss. Paul is great indeed: but however far upward he stretches his mouth, even if he extends himself as far as the third heaven, it is nevertheless necessary that he remain short of the mouth of the Most High, and, content with his own measure, stay within himself; and since he will not be able to reach the face of glory, let him humbly ask that it stoop down to him, and that a kiss be sent across from on high. But he who did not consider it robbery to be equal to God (Phil. 2:6), so as to dare to say, 'I and the Father are one,' because he is joined on equal terms and embraces on equal terms, does not beg a kiss from a lower place, but joins mouth to mouth at an equal height, and by a singular prerogative takes the kiss from the mouth. For Christ, therefore, the kiss is the fullness; for Paul, a participation: so that while the one glories that he has been kissed from the mouth, the other glories only that he has been kissed from the kiss.
8.9: Happy, nonetheless, the kiss through which not only is God known, but the Father is also loved: who is by no means fully known unless he is perfectly loved. Which soul among you has at some time felt, in the secret of her conscience, the Spirit of the Son crying: 'Abba, Father'? (Gal. 4:6.) She, she, let her presume that she is loved with a father's affection, who feels herself affected by the same Spirit as the Son also. Be confident, whoever you are that are such, be confident, hesitating in nothing. In the Spirit of the Son recognize yourself as a daughter of the Father, a bride or a sister of the Son. By both names you will find her who is of this sort called. It is at hand from which I may prove it; I shall not labor much. It is the voice of the bridegroom to her: 'I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride' (Song 5:1). She is a sister, indeed, because from one Father; a bride, because in one Spirit. For if a carnal marriage constitutes two in one flesh, why shall a spiritual union not rather join two in one spirit? For he who clings to the Lord is one spirit (1 Cor. 6:17). But hear also concerning the Father, how lovingly and how graciously he both names her daughter and nonetheless invites her, as his own daughter-in-law, to the tender embraces of the Son. 'Hear, O daughter,' he says, 'and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and the house of your father, and the king shall desire your beauty' (Ps. 45:10, 11). See from whom she so earnestly asks the kiss. O holy soul, have reverence, since he himself is the Lord your God, and perhaps is not to be kissed, but to be adored, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, unto ages of ages. Amen.

9.1: Let us now come to the book, and give a reason and a sequence to the words of the bride. For they hang, and nod, broken off, without a beginning. And therefore something must be set before them to which they may fittingly cohere. Let us suppose, then, that these whom we have called the companions of the bridegroom, for the sake of visiting and greeting her, as yesterday and the day before, have now also come to the bride; and have found her murmuring under her breath and weary, and that they wonder at the cause, and address her, as it were, in this manner. What new thing has happened? why do we see you sadder than usual? what is the cause of this unexpected murmuring? Surely, when you were going away, turned aside and estranged, after your lovers, with whom it was ill with you, compelled at last to return to your former husband, did you not press on with many prayers and tears, that you might at least deserve to touch his feet? I remember, she says. What? When you had obtained that, and at the same time received, in the kiss of the feet, pardon for your offenses, were you not again made impatient, and by no means content with so great a condescension, but desirous of a greater familiarity, and did you not ask, with the same insistence as before, a second grace also, and obtain it, so that in the kiss of the hand you acquired virtues not few, and not small? I do not deny it, she says. And they: But indeed, are you not the one who used to swear and protest that if it were ever granted you to arrive at the kiss of the hand, it would now be enough for you, and that you would ask nothing further? I am she. What then? Will you perhaps complain that something of the things you had received has been taken away? Nothing. Or do you fear that what you had presumed was pardoned you, concerning your former evil way of life, is going to be demanded back? No.
9.2: Come then, tell us from what we can satisfy you. I do not rest, she says, unless he kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. Thanks for the kiss of the feet, thanks also for that of the hand; but if he has any care for me, 'Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth' (Song 1:1). I am not ungrateful, but I love. I have received, I confess, things greater than my merits, but altogether lower than my desires. I am carried by desire, not by reason. Do not, I ask, complain of presumption, where affection urges. Modesty, certainly, protests; but love overcomes. Nor am I ignorant that the honor of the king loves judgment (Ps. 99:4); but headlong love neither waits for judgment, nor is tempered by counsel, nor is bridled by shame, nor is subjected to reason. I ask, I beseech, I demand, let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. See, by his grace I have now for many years taken care to live chastely and soberly, I apply myself to reading, I resist vices, I give myself often to prayer; I watch against temptations, I reconsider my years in the bitterness of my soul. Without complaint, as I think, so far as in me lies, I conduct myself among the brethren; I am subject to the higher powers; going out and coming in at the command of the elder. I do not covet the things of others; rather I have given what is mine, and myself as well. In the sweat of my face I eat my bread: but for the rest, whatever there is in all these things consists wholly of custom, and nothing of sweetness. What am I but, according to the prophet, the heifer Ephraim, taught to love the threshing? (Hos. 10:11.) Finally, in the Gospel, he who does only what he ought to do is reputed a useless servant (Luke 17:10). The commandments, perhaps, I fulfill in some fashion; but my soul is as earth without water in them. That my burnt offering, then, may be made fat: let him kiss me, I ask, with the kiss of his mouth.
9.3: Very many of you, as I recall, are also accustomed to complain to me, in their private confessions, of a languor of soul dry in this way, and of a dullness of a stolid mind: that they cannot, namely, penetrate the high and subtle things of God, that of the sweetness of the spirit they feel either nothing or little. What are these but sighs for the kiss? They sigh, plainly, and they gape after the spirit of wisdom and of understanding: of understanding, surely, that by it they may reach; of wisdom, that they may taste what they have grasped by the understanding. I think that the prophet prayed in this very affection when he said: 'Let my soul be filled as with fat and with richness, and my mouth will praise with lips of exultation' (Ps. 63:5). He was asking altogether for a kiss, and for that kiss at whose touch, the lips having been steeped in the fatness of a special grace, there would follow what the same man asks elsewhere: 'Let my mouth be filled with praise, that I may sing your glory, your greatness all the day' (Ps. 71:8). And finally he poured it out when he had tasted: 'How great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you' (Ps. 31:19). This kiss has detained us long enough, and I do not yet trust, to tell the truth, that I have expressed it worthily enough. But let us pass on to what remains, because it becomes known better when impressed than when expressed.
9.4: There follows: 'For your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the best ointments' (Song 1:1, 2). And whose words these are, the author does not say, leaving it to us freely to consider to which person they most fittingly belong. But I do not lack that from which I may fittingly assign them either to the bride, or to the bridegroom, or even to the companions of the bridegroom. And first I will show how they fit the bride. Meanwhile, while she and they were conversing together, he himself drew near, of whom the talk was. He certainly draws near gladly to those who are speaking of him. So he is accustomed to do. So, to those going to Emmaus and conferring among themselves, he showed himself a pleasant and eloquent companion (Luke 24:15). For this is what he promises in the Gospel: 'Where two or three have been gathered in my name, I am in the midst of them' (Matt. 18:20); and through the prophet: 'Before they cry out,' he says, 'I will hear; and while they are still speaking I will say: Behold, I am present' (Isa. 65:24). So, then, now, uncalled, he was present, and, delighted by the words, he came before the prayers. I think that sometimes he does not even wait for words, but is summoned by thoughts alone. For the man who was found according to the heart of God says: 'The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart' (Ps. 10:17). Give heed to yourselves, you also, in every place, knowing that he knows all your things, God who searches hearts and reins, who has fashioned your hearts one by one and understands all your works. The bride, then, perceiving that the bridegroom is present, stopped short (for she is ashamed of the presumption in which she understands herself to have been caught, since she had thought it more modest to attempt this through intermediaries); and soon, turning to him, she tries, as best she can, to excuse the boldness: 'For better,' she says, 'are your breasts than wine, fragrant with the best ointments.' As if she should say: If I seem to be wise unto high things, you have done it, O bridegroom, you who have nursed me with so great a condescension in the sweetness of your breasts, so that, every fear driven out by love of you, not by my own boldness, I dare perhaps more than is expedient. I dare, certainly, mindful of the kindness, unmindful of the majesty. Let these things have been said for the sequence of the words.
9.5: Now let us see of what sort this commendation of the bridegroom's breasts is. The two breasts of the bridegroom are two proofs in him of inborn gentleness: that he both waits patiently for the one who fails, and receives kindly the one who repents. A twofold sweetness, I say, of pleasantness overflows in the breast of the Lord Jesus: long-suffering, namely, in waiting, and readiness in giving. And hear that this is not my own invention. You read, surely, of the long-suffering: 'Do you despise the riches of his goodness, and patience, and long-suffering?' Likewise: 'Or do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?' (Rom. 2:4.) For to this end he long suspends the sentence of vengeance from the one who despises, that at some time he may show the grace of remission in the one who repents. For he does not will the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. Let us set down examples also of the other breast, which has been called readiness to forgive. You read also of it: 'In whatever hour the sinner groans, his sin shall be forgiven him' (Ezek. 33:11, 12); you read: 'Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is great in pardoning' (Isa. 55:7). David beautifully comprises both in a few words, saying: 'Long-suffering, and abundant in mercy' (Ps. 103:8). By the experience, then, of this twofold goodness the bride confesses that she has grown into such confidence as to dare to ask for the kiss. What wonder, she says, if I presume thus of you, O bridegroom, I who have experienced so great an abundance of sweetness from your breasts? It is the sweetness of your breasts, then, that provokes me to daring, not confidence in my own merits.
9.6: But as to what she says, 'Your breasts are better than wine,' this is the meaning. The fatness of grace which flows from your breasts is more effective for me unto spiritual progress than the biting imprecation of prelates. Nor are they only better than wine, but also fragrant with the best ointments; because you not only nourish those present with the milk of inward sweetness, but you also sprinkle the absent with the grateful odor of a good reputation, having a good testimony both from those who are within and from those who are without. You have, I say, milk within, and ointments without; since indeed there would be none whom you might refresh with milk, if you did not first draw them by the odor. Certainly, concerning these ointments, if they contain anything worthy of consideration, it will be seen after this, when we have come to the place where she says in what follows: 'In the odor of your ointments we will run' (Song 1:3). Now, according to our promise, let us see whether these same words, which have been given to the bride, fit the bridegroom also.
9.7: While the bride was speaking of the bridegroom, suddenly, as I had said, he is present, he nods to her desire, he gives the kiss, and he fulfills in her the word that is written: 'You have given him the desire of his heart, and you have not defrauded him of the request of his lips' (Ps. 21:2). Which the filling of her breasts also proves. For of such efficacy is the holy kiss, that from it, as soon as she has received it, the bride conceives, her breasts swelling, surely, and growing fat, as it were, with milk, in testimony. Those whose study it is to pray often have experienced what I say. Often we approach the altar with a heart lukewarm and dry, and we apply ourselves to prayer. But as we persist, grace is suddenly poured in, the breast grows fat, a flood of piety fills the inward parts; and if there is someone to press them, they will not be slow to pour out abundantly the milk of the sweetness conceived. Let him say, then: You have, O bride, what you asked, and this is a sign to you, that your breasts have been made better than wine. By this, namely, you may know that you have received the kiss, that you feel you have conceived. Whence your breasts also have swollen, made, in the abundance of milk, better than the wine of secular knowledge, which indeed intoxicates, but with curiosity, not with charity; filling, not nourishing; puffing up, not building up; gorging, not strengthening.
9.8: But let us allow the companions also to bring these words forth. Unjustly, they say, do you murmur against the bridegroom; because what he has already given is worth more than what you ask. For what you demand delights you, indeed; but the breasts with which you nourish the little ones, whom you also bear, are better, that is, more necessary, than the wine of contemplation. For it is one thing that gladdens the heart of one man, and another that builds up many. For although Rachel is more beautiful, Leah is more fruitful. Do not, then, press too hard upon the kisses of contemplation, because the breasts of preaching are better.
9.9: Another sense also occurs, which I had not indeed proposed, but I will by no means pass it by. For why should we not say that these words fit rather those very ones over whom she presides in solicitude, as a mother or a nurse over little ones? For the young women, and souls still tender, do not bear it with equanimity that she should be free for quiet, by whose teaching they desire to be more fully instructed, and by whose examples formed. Is not, finally, the restlessness of such as these checked in what follows, where, under a grave protest, they are forbidden to awaken the beloved until she herself wills? (Song 2:7.) These, then, perceiving that the bride is gaping after kisses, seeking privacy for herself, fleeing the public, declining the crowds, and preferring her own quiet to their care: 'Do not,' they say, 'do not; because greater fruit exists in the breasts than in the embraces.' For by them you vindicate us from the carnal desires which war against the soul; you rescue us from the world, and you gain us for God. This, then, is what they say: 'Because your breasts are better than wine.' The pleasure of the flesh, they say, by which a little before we were held, drunk as with wine, is overcome by these spiritual delights which your breasts drop for us.
9.10: And beautifully they compare carnal affection to wine. For as the grape, once pressed, no longer has anything to pour out a second time, but is condemned to a perpetual dryness, so the flesh, in the pressing of death, is dried of all its delight entirely, nor does it grow green again unto lusts. Whence the prophet: 'All flesh is grass, and all its glory as the flower of the grass.' 'The grass has dried up, and the flower has fallen' (Isa. 40:6, 7); and the Apostle: 'He who sows in the flesh will of the flesh also reap corruption' (Gal. 6:8); and again: 'Foods for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both this and them' (1 Cor. 6:13). But see whether this proportion does not perhaps fit not the flesh only, but the world as well. For it too passes, and its concupiscence: and although all things that are in the world have an end, their end will not be an end. But the breasts are not so. For these, when they have been exhausted, again take from the fountain of the maternal breast that which they may give to drink to those who suck. Rightly, then, are the breasts of the bride asserted to be better than the love of the flesh or of the world, which are never dried up by any number of nursing ones, but always abound from the inward parts of charity, so that they may flow again. For rivers flow from her belly, and there comes to be in her a fountain of living water springing up into eternal life (John 7:38; 4:14). The praise of the breasts is heaped up, further, by the fragrance of the ointments, because they not only feed by the savor of words, but also breathe sweetly by the reputation of deeds. Now what the breasts are, with what milk they are swollen, with what ointments anointed, we will show, Christ helping, under another beginning of the sermon: who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

10.1: I am not of a deep understanding, nor of so clear a wit that I can invent anything new out of myself; but there is a great and unfailing fountain, the mouth of Paul, which lies open toward us. From it I draw for myself even now, in the showing of the bride's breasts, as I am often accustomed to do. 'Rejoice,' he says, 'with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep' (Rom. 12:15). The affections of a mother are briefly expressed, because little ones can neither grieve nor be well without her who bore them: on both sides it is necessary that she be conformed to them in her inward parts. I will assign, therefore, according to the opinion of Paul, those two affections to the two breasts of the bride: compassion to one, and congratulation to the other. Otherwise she is little, and not yet of marriageable age, if she has not yet put forth breasts, if, namely, she feels herself neither prompt to rejoice with others nor inclined to grieve with them. Such a one, if she happens to be taken up to the ruling of souls, or to the office of preaching, is of no profit indeed to others, but is a great hindrance to herself. Further, to thrust oneself forward, of how great an impudence is it?
10.2: But let us return to the breasts of the bride, and, according to the diversity of the breasts, let us set forth diverse kinds of milk as well. For congratulation pours the milk of exhortation, but compassion the milk of consolation. Further, the spiritual mother feels each kind abundantly bedewed from heaven upon her pious breast as often as she receives the kiss. You may see her soon, with full breasts, bend over the little ones to be nursed; and from the one, indeed, minister more abundantly things of consolation, but from the other things of exhortation, according as she sees them suit each one. For example, if she has caught one of those whom she has begotten in the Gospel shaken by some strong temptation, and troubled and sad on that account, and made fainthearted, no longer able to bear the force of the temptation: how she grieves with him, how she soothes him! how she laments, how she consoles him! how many arguments of piety she soon finds, by which she may raise up the desolate one! On the contrary, if she has recognized him as prompt, as eager, as progressing well, she exults, she approaches him with wholesome warnings, she kindles him further, she instructs him in whatever she can, that he may persevere, and she exhorts him that he may always progress unto what is better. She conforms herself to all, she transfers into herself the affections of all, and finally she proves herself a mother no less of those who are failing than of those who are progressing.
10.3: How many today show themselves affected otherwise? of these I speak, who have undertaken to rule souls. For what cannot be said without a miserable groaning, they melt down in the furnace of avarice the reproaches of Christ, the spittings, the scourges, the nails, the lance, the cross, and the death, all these things, and they squander them in the acquisition of shameful gain, and they hasten to shut up the price of the universe in their purses: differing, certainly, from Judas Iscariot in this alone, that he balanced the whole profit of these things against a number of a few denarii, while these, with a more voracious gluttony for gains, demand infinite sums of money. These they gape after with an insatiable desire; for these, lest they lose them, they fear; and when they lose them, they grieve; in the love of these they rest, so far at least as they are free from the care of keeping them or of increasing them. Neither the fall of souls is reckoned, nor their salvation. They are surely not mothers, who, although they have grown excessively fat, gross, and wide from the patrimony of the Crucified, do not suffer with him over the destruction of Joseph. She who is a mother does not dissemble: she has breasts, and they are not empty. She knows how to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep, nor does she cease to press out from the breast of congratulation the milk of exhortation, and from the breast of compassion the milk of consolation. And concerning the breasts of the bride, or the milk of the breasts, let these things suffice.
10.4: Now with what ointments those same breasts also breathe sweetly, I will show, if only I am helped by your prayers, so that what has been given me to perceive about it may also be given me to speak worthily, for the profit of those who hear. The ointments of the bridegroom are one thing, and those of the bride another, just as each also has breasts of his own. But the place in which those of the bridegroom are to be treated has been marked out above: now let us attend to the ointments of the bride, and that more attentively, as to things which Scripture has commended not moderately, so as to pronounce them not simply good, but the best. And I set down different kinds of ointments, so that from the several we may choose those which most of all suit the breasts of the bride. There is an ointment of contrition, and there is an ointment of devotion, and there is one of piety. The first is pungent, causing pain; the second tempering, soothing pain; the third healing, even driving out the disease. Now let us discuss each more at large.
10.5: There is, then, an ointment which the soul entangled in many crimes compounds for herself, if, when she begins to think upon her ways, she gathers, heaps up, and pounds together in the mortar of conscience many and various kinds of her sins, and cooks them all together in the pot of a burning breast with a certain fire of penitence and of sorrow, so that she can say with the prophet: 'My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire will blaze up' (Ps. 39:3). See, this is one ointment with which the sinful soul ought to season the beginnings of her conversion, and to apply it to her wounds while they are fresh. For the first sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit. So long, then, as she does not have, being poor and needy, that from which she may compound for herself a better and more precious ointment, let her not neglect to prepare this one in the meantime, although from cheap kinds; because a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise (Ps. 51:17). But it will appear the less cheap to the divine regards, the more she has become cheap to herself in the remembrance of her sins.
10.6: Yet if we say that by that visible ointment, with which the bodily feet of God are related in the Gospel to have been visibly anointed by the sinful woman, this invisible and spiritual one was figured, we shall not be able to repute it altogether cheap. For what is read of that one? 'And the house,' it says, 'was filled with the odor of the ointment' (John 12:3). It was dripping from the hands of the sinful woman, and was poured upon the outermost members of the body, that is, the feet: and yet it was not so contemptible or cheap but that the strength of the spices and the sweetness of the odor filled the whole house. But if we consider how great a fragrance is sprinkled upon the Church in the conversion of one sinner, and how great an odor of life unto life any penitent becomes, if he does penance publicly and perfectly, we shall surely pronounce with equal certainty of this one also, that the house was filled with the odor of the ointment. And finally the odor of penitence reaches even the mansions of the blessed above, so that, the Truth herself bearing witness, there is great joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance (Luke 15:10). Rejoice, you penitents; you fainthearted, be strengthened. I say to you, whom, lately converted from the world and withdrawing from your depraved ways, the bitterness and confusion of a penitent mind soon received, and whom the excessive pain, as it were, of wounds still fresh tortures and disturbs. Let your hands securely drip the bitterness of myrrh into this wholesome anointing, because a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise. An anointing of this sort is by no means to be spurned, nor esteemed cheap, whose odor not only stirs men to correction, but also invites the angels to exultation.
10.7: But there is an ointment more precious, surely, than that one by as much as it is compounded of better kinds. The kinds of this one, indeed, lest they be sought far off, we find in our own possession and without difficulty, and from our own little gardens we quite easily take a supply of such things, as often as necessity demands. For who does not have sufficiently at hand, from what is his own, when he wishes, iniquities and sins, if he does not dissemble? But these, as you recognize, are the kinds of the first ointment, which we have already described. But the spices of this second one our earth by no means produces; rather we seek them out for ourselves from afar and from the farthest ends. For every best gift, and every perfect gift, is from above, descending from the Father of lights (James 1:17). For this ointment is made from the divine benefits conferred upon the human race. Happy is he who takes care to gather them studiously for himself, and to bring them back before the eyes of his mind with worthy thanksgiving. Surely, when they have been bruised and pounded in the vessel of the breast with the pestle of frequent meditation, then all cooked together with the fire of holy desire, and at last enriched with the oil of gladness, there will be an anointing far more precious and more excellent than the former. To prove it, the testimony of him who says, 'The sacrifice of praise will honor me,' suffices (Ps. 50:23). Nor is there any doubt that the remembrance of benefits stirs one up to praise.
10.8: Further, since Scripture testifies of that other one only this, that it is by no means despised, it is clear that the one which also honors is more greatly commended. For that one is applied to the feet, this one to the head. For if in Christ the head is to be referred to the divinity, Paul saying, 'The head of Christ is God' (1 Cor. 11:3), without doubt he anoints the head who gives thanks, since he touches God, not man. Not that he is not man who is God, since God and man are one Christ; but because every good is from God, not from man, even that very good which is ministered through man. For surely it is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing (John 6:63). For this reason he also is cursed who puts his hope in man (Jer. 17:5); since, although our whole hope rightly hangs upon the man who is God, yet not because he is man, but because he is God. And so that ointment is offered to the feet, this one to the head; since both the humiliation of a contrite heart accords with the humility of the flesh, and glorification befits the majesty. See what an ointment I have set before you, with which that dreadful head does not, surely, consider it unworthy to be touched by princes, but rather judges it a mark of honor, saying: 'The sacrifice of praise will honor me.'
10.9: Wherefore it does not belong to a soul that is poor and needy, or small of heart, to compound an anointing of this sort, for its spices and kinds are possessed by confidence alone, yet a confidence which descends from liberty of spirit and purity of heart. For a mind that is fainthearted and of little faith is constrained by the scantiness of its own household store, nor, because of its poverty, is it able to be at leisure for attending to the divine praises, or for looking upon those benefits which give birth to praises. And if at some time it certainly tries to rise, it is at once called back to its own affairs by the pressing cares of domestic necessities, and is compelled by its own want to be kept down within itself. But if the cause of this misery is sought from me, I will say what you yourselves, unless I am mistaken, will recognize either to be, or to have been, in you. For two causes, it seems to me, a sickness of soul of this sort and a diffidence are accustomed to come about: either, namely, from the newness of conversion, or else from lukewarmness of conduct, even if one has had a long time in the conversion. Each, surely, humbles and casts down the conscience, and makes it unquiet, while, whether on account of the time or on account of the lukewarmness, it feels the old passions of the soul not yet dead within itself: and, having need, accordingly, to attend to cutting away from the garden of the heart the thorns of iniquities and the nettles of cupidities, it is not permitted to wander farther from itself. What then? can he who labors in his groaning at the same time also exult in the praises of God? In what way will there sound together, in the mouth of one groaning and lamenting, that word of Isaiah, namely thanksgiving, and the voice of praise (Isa. 51:3)? For, as we receive from the Wise Man: 'Music in mourning is an unseasonable narration' (Sir. 22:6). Finally, thanksgiving follows a benefit; it does not go before it. But the soul which is still in sadness does not rejoice in a benefit, but stands in need of one. She has, then, that from which she may offer prayers, but not that from which she may return thanks. For how will she recall a benefit which she has not received? Rightly, then, did I say that it does not belong to a poor soul to compound this ointment, which ought to be composed of the divine benefits called to mind; since she cannot see the light so long as she is looking at the darkness. For she is in bitterness, and the sad remembrance of sins occupies the memory, nor is it pleasing to admit anything joyful at the same time. For this reason the prophetic spirit announces to such as these, saying: 'It is vain for you to rise before the light' (Ps. 127:2); which is: in vain do you rise to look upon the benefits which delight, unless the light of consolation has first been received from the guilt which troubles. This ointment, then, does not belong to the poor.
10.10: But see who they are that not unfittingly glory in an abundance of it. The apostles went rejoicing from the sight of the council, because they had been counted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41). They had surely instilled into themselves much of the fatness of the spirit, they whose gentleness yielded, I do not say to words, but not even to stripes. For they were rich in charity, which is exhausted by no expenditures, and from it they were sufficient easily to offer marrowy whole burnt offerings. Their sweating breasts poured out everywhere the holy liquor with which they had been more fully imbued, when they were speaking in various tongues the mighty works of God, according as the Holy Spirit gave them to speak (Acts 2:11, 4). Nor is there any doubt that those also abounded in the same ointments to whom the Apostle bore witness, saying: 'I give thanks to my God always for you, in the grace of God which has been given you in Christ Jesus; because in all things you have been made rich in him, in every word and in all knowledge, as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you, so that nothing is lacking to you in any grace' (1 Cor. 1:4-7). Would that I too might return these very thanks for you, that I may see you rich in virtues, eager in the praises of God, overflowing more abundantly with this spiritual fatness, in Christ Jesus our Lord.

11.1: I said at the end of the sermon, and it does not irk me to repeat it, that I desire you all to be made partakers of the sacred anointing, that one, namely, in which holy devotion calls to mind the benefits of God with joy and thanksgiving. For this is good, both for the lightening of the labors of the present life, which certainly become more tolerable for us when we exult in the praise of God; and because nothing so properly represents on earth a certain state of the heavenly habitation as the eagerness of those who praise God, Scripture saying: 'Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you unto ages of ages' (Ps. 84:4). Of this ointment especially I think the prophet said: 'Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity, like ointment on the head' (Ps. 133:1). Nor does it seem able to fit the former one. For that one, although it is good, is nevertheless not pleasant; because the remembrance of sins makes bitterness, not pleasantness. But neither do those who make that one dwell in unity, since each one mourns and laments his own sins. But those who are occupied in thanksgiving look upon and think of God alone; and on this account they themselves truly dwell in unity. But what they do is good, because they keep the glory most justly for him whose it is, and nonetheless pleasant, because it delights.
11.2: Wherefore I urge you, my friends, to turn your foot back at times from the troublesome and anxious remembrance of your own ways, and to escape into the smoother paths of a more serene memory of the benefits of God, so that you who are confounded in yourselves may breathe again at the sight of him. I wish you to experience that which the holy prophet counsels, saying: 'Take delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart' (Ps. 37:4). And sorrow for sins is indeed necessary, but not if it is continual. Let it certainly be interrupted by a more joyful remembrance of the divine kindness, lest perhaps the heart be hardened by sadness, and perish the more by despair. Let us mix honey with the wormwood, so that a wholesome bitterness may then be able to give health, when, tempered by an admixture of sweetness, it can be drunk. Hear, finally, how God himself tempers the bitterness of a contrite heart, how he calls the fainthearted back from the pit of despair, how with the honey of a gentle and faithful promise he consoles the one who mourns and raises up the one who distrusts. He says through the prophet: 'I will bridle your mouth with my praise, lest you perish' (Isa. 48:9). That is: lest, at the sight of your crimes, you fall into too great a sadness, and, despairing like an unbridled horse, rush headlong and perish; with the bridle, he says, of my indulgence I will hold you in, and I will raise you up with my praises, and you will breathe again in my good things, you who are confounded by your own evils, when you find me, certainly, more kind than you are blameworthy. If Cain had been bridled with this bridle, he would by no means have said in despair: 'My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve pardon' (Gen. 4:13). Far be it, far be it. For his kindness is greater than any iniquity whatever. Therefore the just man is an accuser of himself not continually, but only at the beginning of his speech (Prov. 18:17): but further, he is accustomed to close the end of his speech in the praises of God. See, finally, the just man proceeding in this order. 'I have thought,' he says, 'upon my ways, and I have turned my feet unto your testimonies' (Ps. 119:59): so that he who, namely, had suffered contrition and unhappiness in his own ways might take delight in the way of the testimonies of God, as in all riches. You also, therefore, after the example of the just man, if you think of yourselves in humility, think also of the Lord in goodness. For so you read in the Wise Man: 'Think of the Lord in goodness, and in simplicity of heart seek him' (Wis. 1:1). But frequent, or rather continual, remembrance of the divine munificence easily persuades the mind of this. Otherwise, how shall that word of the Apostle be fulfilled, 'In all things giving thanks' (1 Thess. 5:18), if the things for which thanks are owed have withdrawn from the heart? I do not want you to be marked with the Jewish reproach, of whom Scripture testifies that they were not mindful of his benefits, and of his wonders which he showed them (Ps. 78:11).
11.3: But because it is impossible for every man to call to mind and to gather together all the good things which the merciful and pitying Lord does not cease to bestow upon mortals (for who shall tell the powers of the Lord, or make all his praises heard? (Ps. 106:2), at least that which is chief and greatest, the work, namely, of our redemption, should not depart in any measure from the memory of the redeemed. In this work I will take care to press upon your studies two things especially, which now occur. And this as briefly as I shall be able, by way of a summary, mindful of that sentence: 'Give an occasion to a wise man, and he will be wiser' (Prov. 9:9). Those two things, then, are the manner and the fruit. And the manner is the emptying of God; the fruit, our being filled from him. To meditate on this is a seedbed of holy hope; that, an incentive of the highest love. Both are necessary to our progress, lest either hope be mercenary, if it is not accompanied by love; or love grow lukewarm, if it is thought to be without fruit.
11.4: Further, we look for such a fruit of our love as he himself whom we love has promised: 'A measure,' he says, 'full, and pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, they will give into your bosom' (Luke 6:38). This measure, as I hear, will be without measure. But I would like to know of what thing that measure is to be, or rather that immensity which is promised. 'The eye has not seen, O God, without you, the things you have prepared for those who love you' (Isa. 64:4). Tell us, you who prepare, what you prepare. We believe, we trust, that it is truly as you promise: 'We shall be filled with the good things of your house' (Ps. 65:4). But with what good things, I ask, or of what sort? Perhaps with grain, wine, and oil, with gold and silver, or with precious stones? But these we have known and have seen; and we see them, and we are weary of them. We seek that which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man. This pleases, this has savor, this delights to inquire into, whatever it is. 'They shall all,' he says, 'be teachable of God' (John 6:45), and he himself will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28). As I hear it, the fullness which we look for from God will be nothing other than of God.
11.5: But who can grasp how great a multitude of sweetness is comprised in this brief word: 'God will be all in all'? That I may say nothing of the body, I look at three things in the soul: reason, will, memory; and these three are the soul itself. How much is lacking to each of these, in the present age, of its own integrity and perfection, everyone feels who walks in the spirit. Why is this, if not because God is not yet all in all? Hence it is that reason also is very often deceived in its judgments, and the will is tossed by a fourfold disturbance, and the memory is confounded by a manifold forgetfulness. To this threefold vanity the noble creature has been subjected, not willingly, yet in hope. For he who fills with good things the desire of the soul, he himself will be for the reason a fullness of light, for the will a multitude of peace, for the memory a continuance of eternity. O truth, charity, eternity! O blessed and beatifying Trinity! to you my miserable trinity sighs most miserably, because it is unhappily in exile from you. Departing from you, in how many errors, sorrows, and fears has it entangled itself! Alas for me! what a trinity we have exchanged for you! 'My heart is troubled,' and thence sorrow; 'my strength has left me,' and thence fear; 'and the light of my eyes is not with me' (Ps. 38:10), and thence error. See how unlike a trinity, O trinity of my soul, you have shown in your exile.
11.6: But why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I will still confess to him (Ps. 42:5); when, namely, error has withdrawn from the reason, sorrow from the will, and all fear from the memory, and there has succeeded that wonderful serenity which we hope for, a full sweetness, an eternal security. The first of these God as truth will bring about; the second, God as charity; the third, God as supreme power: so that God may be all in all, the reason receiving a light that cannot be extinguished, the will obtaining a peace that cannot be disturbed, the memory clinging eternally to the unfailing fountain. See to it yourselves whether you rightly assign that first one to the Son, the next to the Holy Spirit, and the last to the Father, yet in such a way that you take away none of these either from the Father, or from the Son, or from the Holy Spirit; lest perhaps the distinction diminish the fullness for any of the persons, or the perfection take away what is proper to each. Consider at the same time this also, what the sons of this age experience of a like sort from the allurements of the flesh, from the spectacles of the world, and from the pomps of Satan: although this whole thing is that by which the present life mocks its wretched lovers, John saying: 'Whatever is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, and the concupiscence of the eyes, and the ambition of the world' (1 John 2:16). These things concerning the fruit of redemption.
11.7: In the manner also, which, if you recall, we defined as the emptying of God, I commend to you likewise three things especially to be looked at. For that emptying was not simple or slight; but he emptied himself even unto flesh, unto death, unto the cross (Phil. 2:7, 8). Who can worthily weigh of how great a humility, meekness, and condescension it was that the Lord of majesty should be clothed with flesh, punished with death, disgraced with the cross? But someone says: 'Was the Creator not able to repair his work without this difficulty?' He was able, but he preferred to do it with injury to himself, lest the worst and most hateful vice of ingratitude should any longer find an occasion in man. He took upon himself, certainly, much weariness, whereby he might hold man a debtor of much love; and the difficulty of redemption might put him in mind of thanksgiving, whom the ease of creation had made less devout. For what was man, created and ungrateful, saying? 'I was indeed founded for nothing, but with no burden or labor of the author: for he spoke, and I was made, just as all things also were.' What great thing is it, however great the things you have given, in the ease of a word? Thus human impiety, making light of the benefit of creation, was taking from it the matter of ingratitude, from which it ought to have had a cause of love, and that in order to excuse excuses in sins. But the mouth of those who speak wicked things has been stopped. It is clearer than light how great an expense he has now made for you, O man: from Lord he did not disdain to become a servant, from rich a poor man, flesh from the Word, and from the Son of God the son of man. Remember now that, although you were made from nothing, you were not redeemed from nothing. In six days he founded all things, and you among all things. But for thirty whole years he worked your salvation in the midst of the earth: O how much he labored in enduring! The necessities of the flesh, the temptations of the enemy: did he not weigh them down for himself with the ignominy of the cross, and heap them up with the horror of death? Necessarily, indeed. Thus, thus have you saved men and beasts, O Lord; as you have multiplied your mercy, O God (Ps. 36:6, 7).
11.8: Meditate on these things, turn them over in your minds. With such perfumes refresh your inward parts, which the more troublesome odor of sins has long tormented, so that you may abound in these ointments also, no less sweet than wholesome. Yet do not think that you yet have those best ones, which are commended in the breasts of the bride. The straitness of a sermon that must now be ended forbids us to begin about them just now. Hold in memory the things that have been said about the others, prove them in your life; and concerning these, help me with your prayers, that I may be able to speak worthily what is also worthy of such great delights of the bride, and builds your souls unto the love of the bridegroom, our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
